title: CFM and m³/h: Sizing Ventilation
h1: CFM and m³/h — sizing ductwork across unit systems
description: US HVAC catalogs quote fans in CFM. European catalogs quote in m³/h or L/s. Here is the exact factor and how to size ductwork consistently.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

hero: 1 CFM = 1.699 m³/h = 0.472 L/s. Simple ratios that hide a bigger issue: ventilation codes across regions target very different air-change rates.
body: Fan datasheets, air handlers, VAV boxes and register throws are all sized by volumetric airflow. The US uses cubic feet per minute (CFM). Europe uses cubic metres per hour (m³/h) or litres per second (L/s). ASHRAE and EN both specify minimum ventilation rates — but in different units and with different assumptions.

ASHRAE 62.1: minimum 5 CFM/person + 0.06 CFM/ft² for offices (about 7.5 L/s + 0.3 L/s·m²). EN 16798: 10 L/s/person for good IAQ (Category II). These translate to roughly comparable per-person rates but the per-area component differs materially — a European engineer sizing to EN often exceeds ASHRAE minimums.

ACH = fresh air rate / room volume. A 40 m² office at 3 m ceiling = 120 m³. Ventilating at 60 L/s = 216 m³/h gives 1.8 ACH. ASHRAE typically results in 0.5–1.5 ACH for offices, 4–6 for restaurants, 15+ for laboratories. Same physical rate, three different equivalent expressions (CFM, m³/h, ACH) — engineers switch depending on what the datasheet lists.
## Worked example — a bathroom exhaust fan

US code (IRC): 50 CFM intermittent or 20 CFM continuous for a residential bath. 50 CFM = 85 m³/h = 23.6 L/s. UK Building Regs Part F: 15 L/s for a bath = 54 m³/h = 31.8 CFM. UK spec is 37% lower than US intermittent — reflecting different assumed run times and moisture-load assumptions.
Multiply CFM by 1.7 for m³/h. Multiply CFM by 0.47 for L/s. Ventilation codes agree on per-person rates but diverge on per-area rates.

faqs.q: What is a 'ton' of air conditioning?
faqs.a: 12,000 BTU/hr of cooling = 3.517 kW. Historical: the heat needed to melt 1 short ton of ice in 24 hours. Airflow of a 1-ton system is typically ~400 CFM (680 m³/h).

faqs.q: Why is L/s common in Europe?
faqs.a: EN 16798 chose L/s because per-person ventilation rates land in comfortable single digits. m³/h is more common on equipment datasheets.
Typical supply duct velocity: 4–8 m/s (800–1,600 fpm). Higher = noisier. Sizing charts convert between airflow and duct diameter given a target velocity.
